description: Different forms of democracy and the values that underpin democratic society.
content_html:
What Is Democracy?

Democracy is one of the most important concepts in Citizenship Studies. The word comes from the ancient Greek words demos (people) and kratos (power) — democracy literally means “power of the people.” At its heart, democracy means that those who are governed have a say in how they are governed. Not all democracies work in exactly the same way, so it is important to understand the different forms democracy can take.

Direct and Representative Democracy

In a direct democracy, citizens make decisions themselves. Ancient Athens is the most famous example: free male citizens gathered in an assembly and voted on laws directly. Today, referendums are the closest equivalent to direct democracy in the UK. When the UK held a referendum on EU membership in 2016, every eligible voter had an equal say — the result was 51.9% in favour of leaving and 48.1% in favour of remaining, a factual outcome on which different citizens hold very different views about its significance.

Most modern democracies, including the UK, use representative democracy. Citizens choose MPs, councillors and other officials to represent them and make decisions in their name. The elected representatives are accountable to voters — if voters are unhappy with their performance, they can be voted out at the next election. This system is practical for large, complex societies where direct votes on every issue would be impossible.

Key Fact

Direct democracy involves citizens voting on decisions themselves (e.g. a referendum). Representative democracy involves citizens electing representatives to make decisions on their behalf (e.g. a general election to choose MPs). The UK mainly uses representative democracy but also uses direct democracy through referendums on major constitutional questions.

The Values That Underpin Democracy

Democracy is not just a voting system — it rests on a set of core values without which elections alone are not enough to make a society truly democratic. The AQA specification identifies five values that underpin democracy: rights, responsibilities, freedoms, equality, and the rule of law.

Rights are entitlements that citizens hold, such as the right to free speech, the right to a fair trial, and the right to vote. In the UK, these are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law. Responsibilities are the duties that citizens owe in return — obeying the law, paying taxes, and respecting the rights of others. Rights and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin: a democracy functions only when citizens exercise both.

Freedoms include the freedom to express opinions, to hold a religion, to assemble peacefully, and to access information. These freedoms allow citizens to participate meaningfully in public life. Equality means that all citizens are equal before the law and have an equal right to participate — regardless of race, gender, religion, or class. Historically, this was not always the case in the UK: women only gained equal voting rights with men in 1928, and many other groups faced discrimination that had to be challenged through law and civic action.

Many students assume a referendum is automatically legally binding because “the people have spoken.” In UK constitutional law, this is not automatically the case. Referendums in the UK are advisory unless Parliament passes specific legislation requiring the result to be acted upon. Parliament remains sovereign and can, in principle, choose not to act on a referendum result — though doing so would be politically very difficult. This connects to the concept of the sovereignty of Parliament, which means Parliament is the supreme law-making authority in the UK. The debate about whether referendums should be made legally binding is itself a contested political question, with supporters arguing they better reflect the public will and critics arguing they can bypass parliamentary scrutiny.

The Rule of Law

The rule of law is especially important to democracy. It means that government and officials must act within the law, that laws apply equally to everyone, and that there are independent courts to enforce them. Without the rule of law, a government could change or ignore laws to suit itself. The UK’s judiciary (courts and judges) is independent of the government — this independence protects citizens from arbitrary use of power. The rule of law also includes the principle of the presumption of innocence — a cornerstone of the criminal justice system.

Key Fact

The five values underpinning democracy are: rights (entitlements of citizens), responsibilities (duties citizens owe), freedoms (liberties to act and speak), equality (equal treatment before the law) and the rule of law (no one is above the law). All five must be present for a democracy to be genuine.

One viewpoint is that the UK is a well-established democracy: it has regular free and fair elections, an independent judiciary, a free press, and legal protections for civil liberties. Citizens can stand for election, join parties, and protest peacefully. The Human Rights Act 1998 gives courts the power to declare legislation incompatible with human rights.

A contrasting viewpoint is that the UK’s democracy has significant shortcomings: the unelected House of Lords has legislative power, the First Past the Post electoral system means many votes have little impact on the outcome, and voter turnout has fallen in several recent elections — raising concerns about democratic engagement. Critics also point to the uncodified constitution as a weakness, arguing it leaves too much power in the hands of the executive without sufficient checks. Both viewpoints contain valid arguments and reflect genuine ongoing debates about democratic reform in the UK.

Why Democracy Matters for Citizens

Understanding what democracy is — and what it requires to function — is the starting point for all of GCSE Citizenship Studies. When you study how Parliament works, how elections are run, how pressure groups operate, or how the law protects rights, you are exploring the practical machinery of democracy. Active citizenship is about citizens taking the values of democracy seriously: participating, holding power to account, and working to make their communities fairer.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Discuss’ question about democracy, always present two contrasting viewpoints and use connectives such as “however,” “on the other hand,” or “in contrast” to show you are weighing the argument rather than just listing points. For a 12-mark ‘Evaluate,’ name at least one real-world example on each side — for example, the Human Rights Act 1998 as evidence of rights protection, or concerns about low voter turnout as evidence of weaknesses. Reach a clear substantiated judgement in your conclusion: “On balance, I argue X because …” A common mistake is writing only about one viewpoint — this caps your answer in the Developing band. Another frequent error is confusing a referendum (which may be advisory) with a legally binding vote: make sure you distinguish these.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Democracy means power ultimately rests with the people; the UK mainly uses representative democracy (elections) but also direct democracy through referendums.
  • Five values underpin democracy: rights, responsibilities, freedoms, equality and the rule of law — all five are needed for democracy to function genuinely.
  • UK referendums are advisory, not automatically legally binding, because Parliament retains sovereignty; the question of whether the UK’s democracy is fully functioning is a legitimate contested debate with arguments on both sides.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes representative democracy?
A) Citizens vote directly on every law and policy
B) Citizens elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf
C) A monarch makes laws on behalf of the people
D) A committee of experts decides government policy
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B) Citizens elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf.

practice_questions.text: Identify two values that underpin democracy in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two of: rights / responsibilities / freedoms / equality / rule of law. Near-duplicate answers (e.g. 'freedom' and 'civil liberties' without development) score 1 mark only. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the rule of law is important in a democratic society.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. A strong answer will include: a clear point identifying what the rule of law means (1 mark), a developed explanation of why it matters — e.g. it prevents governments from acting arbitrarily or above the law (1 mark), a linked consequence such as protecting citizens' rights or maintaining trust in institutions (1 mark), and a real-world anchor or example such as the independence of the judiciary or the Human Rights Act 1998 (1 mark). A single well-developed point with cause and consequence can score 3 of 4; two thin undeveloped points typically score 2.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A 2024 survey conducted by a civic engagement charity found that only 34% of 18-24 year olds said they felt their vote made a difference in a general election, compared with 61% of those aged 55 and over. The charity's director commented: 'Young people are not disengaged from politics — they are disengaged from a system they feel does not represent them.'"

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does the source suggest about the strengths and weaknesses of representative democracy in the UK?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying a specific detail from the source (e.g. only 34% of 18-24 year olds felt their vote made a difference). 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (e.g. the source suggests representative democracy may not be engaging younger citizens effectively). 1 mark for applying own knowledge (e.g. linking to concerns about voter turnout, First Past the Post, or calls for electoral reform). 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that goes beyond the source (e.g. weighing whether this is a structural problem with the system or a matter of civic education, or comparing with participation rates in direct democracy mechanisms such as referendums). Pure summary of the source without interpretation or judgement caps at 1-2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
A local secondary school is considering whether to introduce a school parliament where students vote directly on some school policies, rather than relying on a school council of elected representatives.

Discuss whether direct democracy is better than representative democracy as a way of involving citizens in decision-making.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Presents a well-developed, two-sided discussion using connectives to weigh the argument. Includes at least one named real-world example on each side (e.g. the 2016 EU referendum as an example of direct democracy; general elections and the role of MPs as examples of representative democracy). Uses citizenship vocabulary accurately (sovereignty, mandate, accountability, voter apathy). Reaches a substantiated overall view about which form is better suited to complex decision-making.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both viewpoints present and mostly accurate. At least one named real-world example. Some development of argument rather than mere listing. Some use of connectives.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content but limited development, or largely one-sided. Minimal real-world reference. May describe direct and representative democracy without weighing them.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about one or both forms of democracy. Little or no real-world reference. Descriptive rather than discursive.

practice_questions.text:
'The five values underpinning democracy (rights, responsibilities, freedoms, equality and the rule of law) are all equally important to a functioning democracy.'

Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider arguments for and against the view that all five values are equally important, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained two-sided evaluation that considers multiple values, weighs their relative importance, and names real-world examples (e.g. the Human Rights Act 1998 for rights; the independence of the judiciary for the rule of law; the suffragette movement and the Representation of the People Acts for equality). Reaches a clear substantiated judgement, not merely 'it depends.' May argue that one value is foundational (e.g. the rule of law enables all others) or that all are interdependent. Deploys accurate Citizenship vocabulary throughout.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both viewpoints addressed. At least one named real-world example. A judgement is reached, though it may be less developed or nuanced than Mastering.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some engagement with the statement. Relevant content but limited development or largely one-sided. Some real-world reference, possibly vague.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points about one or two values. Descriptive rather than evaluative. Little or no real-world example or overall judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which form of democracy involves citizens voting directly on decisions, rather than electing representatives?
Which of the following is one of the five values that underpin democracy according to the specification?
In a representative democracy, citizens elect _____ to make decisions on their behalf.
In the UK, referendums are generally considered _____ unless Parliament passes specific legislation requiring the result to be acted upon.
Match each democratic term to its description:
right: Citizens elect representatives to decide on their behalf
Everyone, including government, must obey the law

flashcard_questions.q: What does the word 'democracy' mean in its original Greek roots?
flashcard_questions.a: Power of the people (demos = people, kratos = power).
Citizens vote on decisions themselves, rather than electing representatives.
Citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf.

flashcard_questions.q: Which form of democracy does the UK mainly use?
Give an example of direct democracy used in the UK.
flashcard_questions.a: A referendum, such as the 2016 EU membership referendum.

flashcard_questions.q: Are UK referendum results automatically legally binding?
flashcard_questions.a: No — they are advisory unless Parliament legislates to make them binding.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five values that underpin democracy.
flashcard_questions.a: Rights, responsibilities, freedoms, equality, rule of law.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the rule of law?
flashcard_questions.a: The principle that everyone, including government, is subject to the law.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the presumption of innocence mean in UK law?
flashcard_questions.a: A person is considered innocent until proved guilty by the prosecution.

flashcard_questions.q: When did women gain equal voting rights with men in the UK?
Which 1998 Act incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK domestic law?
What factual outcome did the 2016 UK EU referendum produce?
flashcard_questions.a: 51.9% voted to leave; 48.1% voted to remain.

glossary_terms.definition: A system of government in which power rests with the people, either exercised directly or through elected representatives.
A form of democracy in which citizens vote directly on laws and decisions, rather than electing representatives to decide on their behalf.
A form of democracy in which citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf.
The principle that everyone, including governments and officials, is subject to the law and that no one is above it.
A vote in which all eligible citizens can vote on a single issue; in the UK, referendum results are advisory unless legislation specifically makes them binding.
The legal principle that a person is considered innocent until the prosecution proves their guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

items.title: In Our Time: Democracy (BBC Radio 4)
items.description: Melvyn Bragg and guests explore the origins and development of democracy from ancient Athens to the modern day.

items.title: The Rest Is Politics: Is UK Democracy Working?
items.description: Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart examine the state of UK democracy and what it means for ordinary citizens.

items.title: What did democracy really mean in Athens? (TED-Ed)
items.description: An animated explainer examining how Athenian direct democracy worked and how it differs from modern representative systems.

items.title: GCSE Citizenship: What is Democracy? (Alan's Lessons)
items.description: A focused GCSE revision video covering the key concepts of direct and representative democracy for AQA and Edexcel students.

items.title: The UK Election Results Were the Worst in History (CGP Grey)
items.description: CGP Grey analyses how the First Past the Post system produced deeply disproportionate UK election results, raising questions about democratic representation.

items.title: You Would Be a Terrible Leader (CGP Grey)
items.description: A thought-provoking look at selection bias in democracy and why elections may not always choose the most capable leaders.

items.title: Suffragette (2015)
items.description: Drama following the early UK suffragette movement, showing how women fought for the right to vote and participate in democracy.

items.title: The Trial of the Chicago 7 (2020)
items.description: Aaron Sorkin's film about defendants charged with conspiracy after the 1968 Democratic National Convention protests — a vivid examination of civil liberties and democratic values under pressure.

items.title: BBC Bitesize: Democracy and elections
items.description: Clear GCSE-level revision notes on forms of democracy, how elections work, and the values underpinning democratic society.

items.title: Parliament UK: About Parliament
items.description: The official Parliament website's education pages explaining what Parliament is, what it does, and how the UK's democratic system works.
